Chapter 10: Writing a New Story
If you’ve ever lived with anxiety for years, you probably know how easy it is to feel stuck inside old stories. Maybe it’s that nagging voice that tells you you’re broken, or that you’ll never be free—that anxiety is just part of your life, forever. These stories are powerful. They’re shaped by everything you’ve been through, messages from the world around you, and that relentless inner critic.
But what if you could rewrite that story? The truth is, changing your narrative is not only possible—it’s a deeply human thing to do. It all starts with noticing the old script. Think about those moments when anxiety whispers, “You can’t handle this,” or “You’re not enough.” Instead of simply believing those words, you’ve got a choice. You can pause, question them, and imagine what a different ending might look like.
Picture this: someone starts keeping a journal. Not just to jot down symptoms, but to actually tell a new kind of story. They write about the times they found courage—like making a phone call even though it was scary, or showing up to a gathering when anxiety was loud, or reaching out for help when it felt impossible. Each journal entry becomes its own little act of bravery, a way to take back some control.
Some people change the way they talk about anxiety. Instead of saying, “I am anxious,” they try out, “I’m feeling anxiety right now.” It’s a small tweak, but it creates just a little space between who you are and what you’re feeling. Suddenly, anxiety isn’t your entire identity—it’s something that comes and goes.
Community matters here, too. When you share your story—whether it’s online, in a support group, or just with a close friend—you break that sense of isolation. You start to see you’re not alone. Everybody has their own version of the beast, with their own struggles and victories. And as you connect, the shame starts to fade, replaced by a feeling of solidarity.
And over time, your new story starts to take root. It’s not a fairy tale—there will still be hard days, setbacks, moments when you doubt yourself. But the story is different now. Anxiety isn’t just the villain anymore. It’s a complicated character in a much bigger story. There’s space for hope, for growth, and even for unexpected moments of joy.
Writing a new story is a process. It takes patience, self-compassion, and the courage to start fresh, day after day. But with every page, the beast shrinks a little, and the journey becomes something beautiful, one step at a time.
